claim: Kinetochores are not required for chromosome segregation on acentrosomal spindles in Caenorhabditis elegans oocytes.
source: Surprisingly, kinetochores are not required for chromosome segregation on acentrosomal spindles in Caenorhabditis elegans oocytes, but the mechanism driving chromosomes apart in their absence is not understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Dumont et al., 2010) as stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Lateral microtubule–chromosome associations established during prometaphase remain intact during anaphase to facilitate separation in C. elegans oocytes.
source: In this study, we show that lateral microtubule–chromosome associations established during prometaphase remain intact during anaphase to facilitate separation, defining a novel form of kinetochore-independent segregation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Chromosome dynamics during congression and segregation are controlled by opposing forces in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Chromosome dynamics during congression and segregation are controlled by opposing forces; plus-end directed forces are mediated by a protein complex that forms a ring around the chromosome center and dynein on chromosome arms provides a minus-end force.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from monopolar spindle experiments (Figures 3-5) and metaphase arrest experiments (Figure 4).

claim: Plus-end directed forces are mediated by a protein complex that forms a ring around the chromosome center.
source: Chromosome dynamics during congression and segregation are controlled by opposing forces; plus-end directed forces are mediated by a protein complex that forms a ring around the chromosome center and dynein on chromosome arms provides a minus-end force.
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009) and data from univalent analysis (Figure 6).

claim: Dynein on chromosome arms provides a minus-end force during chromosome segregation.
source: Chromosome dynamics during congression and segregation are controlled by opposing forces; plus-end directed forces are mediated by a protein complex that forms a ring around the chromosome center and dynein on chromosome arms provides a minus-end force.
evidence: This is supported by dynein localization data (Figure 5A-B) and dynein inhibition experiments (Figure 5C-E).

claim: Ring removal at anaphase onset shifts the balance between opposing forces, triggering poleward movement.
source: At anaphase onset, ring removal shifts the balance between these forces, triggering poleward movement along lateral microtubule bundles.
evidence: This is supported by data showing ring dissociation from chromosomes in anaphase (Figure 2) and behavior of chromosomes lacking rings (Figure 6).

claim: Kinetochore components are removed from chromosomes during anaphase in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Despite this fundamental role for the kinetochore in modulating chromosome dynamics, a recent study reported the surprising discovery that kinetochores are not required for chromosome segregation in Caenorhabditis elegans female reproductive cells (oocytes); the authors found that kinetochore components are removed from chromosomes during anaphase, and when they perturbed kinetochore assembly, chromosomes still segregated relatively normally (Dumont et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2010.

claim: When kinetochore assembly is perturbed in C. elegans oocytes, chromosomes still segregate relatively normally.
source: Despite this fundamental role for the kinetochore in modulating chromosome dynamics, a recent study reported the surprising discovery that kinetochores are not required for chromosome segregation in Caenorhabditis elegans female reproductive cells (oocytes); the authors found that kinetochore components are removed from chromosomes during anaphase, and when they perturbed kinetochore assembly, chromosomes still segregated relatively normally (Dumont et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2010.

claim: Oocytes of most species lack centrosomes.
source: Second, oocytes of most species lack centrosomes, which in other cells duplicate and then nucleate and organize microtubules, forming the two spindle poles (Manandhar et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Manandhar et al., 2005.

claim: Microtubules are not nucleated from pre-defined poles in oocytes and instead are sorted and organized into a bipolar structure around the chromosomes.
source: Therefore, microtubules are not nucleated from pre-defined poles in oocytes and instead are sorted and organized into a bipolar structure around the chromosomes (Dumont and Desai, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dumont and Desai, 2012.

claim: Homologous chromosome pairs (bivalents) in mouse oocytes lack end-on kinetochore-microtubule interactions during prometaphase.
source: Work in mouse oocytes has demonstrated that homologous chromosome pairs (bivalents) lack end-on kinetochore-microtubule interactions during prometaphase (Brunet et al., 1999), and stable attachments are not achieved until they have already congressed to the metaphase plate (Kitajima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brunet et al., 1999.

claim: Stable kinetochore-microtubule attachments in mouse oocytes are not achieved until chromosomes have already congressed to the metaphase plate.
source: Work in mouse oocytes has demonstrated that homologous chromosome pairs (bivalents) lack end-on kinetochore-microtubule interactions during prometaphase (Brunet et al., 1999), and stable attachments are not achieved until they have already congressed to the metaphase plate (Kitajima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kitajima et al., 2011.

claim: C. elegans chromosomes are holocentric.
source: C. elegans chromosomes are holocentric, so kinetochore proteins form cup-like structures around the ends of bivalents (in Meiosis I) and sister chromatid pairs (in Meiosis II) (Monen et al., 2005) (Figure 1A, orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Monen et al., 2005.

claim: Kinetochore proteins form cup-like structures around the ends of bivalents in Meiosis I and sister chromatid pairs in Meiosis II in C. elegans.
source: C. elegans chromosomes are holocentric, so kinetochore proteins form cup-like structures around the ends of bivalents (in Meiosis I) and sister chromatid pairs (in Meiosis II) (Monen et al., 2005) (Figure 1A, orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Monen et al., 2005 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Microtubule density is low at chromosome ends in prometaphase in C. elegans oocytes.
source: However, we found that microtubule density is low at chromosome ends in prometaphase and instead lateral microtubule bundles run along the sides of chromosomes (Figure 1A, green).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Lateral microtubule bundles run along the sides of chromosomes in C. elegans oocytes.
source: However, we found that microtubule density is low at chromosome ends in prometaphase and instead lateral microtubule bundles run along the sides of chromosomes (Figure 1A, green).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and previous work (Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009).

claim: The microtubule motor KLP-19 forms a ring around the center of each bivalent in Meiosis I and at the sister chromatid interface in Meiosis II.
source: We also found that the microtubule motor KLP-19 forms a ring around the center of each bivalent (in Meiosis I) and at the sister chromatid interface (in Meiosis II) (Figure 1A, red) and provides a plus-end directed force on the chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: KLP-19 provides a plus-end directed force on chromosomes in C. elegans oocytes.
source: We also found that the microtubule motor KLP-19 forms a ring around the center of each bivalent (in Meiosis I) and at the sister chromatid interface (in Meiosis II) (Figure 1A, red) and provides a plus-end directed force on the chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009).

claim: Chromosome movement on the C. elegans acentrosomal spindle during congression is mediated by movement of chromosomes along laterally associated microtubule bundles, facilitated by plus-end directed forces.
source: Therefore, chromosome movement on the C. elegans acentrosomal spindle during congression is mediated by movement of chromosomes along laterally associated microtubule bundles, facilitated by plus-end directed forces operating on the chromosomes (Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009.

claim: The spindle pole marker KLP-18 remains associated with microtubules throughout anaphase progression in C. elegans oocytes.
source: However, the spindle pole marker KLP-18 remained associated with microtubules throughout anaphase progression despite these morphological changes; the chromosomes moved towards the KLP-18-marked poles and then moved past them in late anaphase (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Chromosomes move towards KLP-18-marked poles and then move past them in late anaphase.
source: However, the spindle pole marker KLP-18 remained associated with microtubules throughout anaphase progression despite these morphological changes; the chromosomes moved towards the KLP-18-marked poles and then moved past them in late anaphase (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ASPM-1 remains at poles during anaphase in C. elegans oocytes.
source: This finding is consistent with earlier work showing that another pole marker, ASPM-1, also remains at poles during anaphase (van der Voet et al., 2009; McNally and McNally, 2011) and with previous lower resolution imaging of KLP-18 localization (Segbert et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van der Voet et al., 2009 and McNally and McNally, 2011.

claim: Spindle poles broaden but remain intact during anaphase in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Therefore, spindle poles broaden but remain intact during anaphase, suggesting that the metaphase microtubule array is reorganized but does not disassemble.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing KLP-18 localization (Figure 1B) and previous work on ASPM-1.

claim: Parallel bundles of microtubules run alongside and extend beyond pairs of separating chromosomes during early- and mid-anaphase in C. elegans oocytes.
source: High-resolution live imaging of oocytes expressing GFP-tubulin and mCherry-histone (to mark microtubules and chromosomes, respectively) revealed parallel bundles of microtubules running alongside and extending beyond pairs of separating chromosomes during early- and mid-anaphase (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Each separating chromosome pair sits within its own channel in the microtubule array, and each of these channels is open from pole to pole during anaphase.
source: Therefore, each separating chromosome pair sits within its own channel in the microtubule array, and each of these channels is open from pole to pole.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution imaging data shown in Figures 1D and 2A, and Videos 1-5.

claim: Six regions of low-microtubule density exist in the anaphase spindle, representing the six sets of separating homologous chromosomes in C. elegans.
source: This imaging revealed six regions of low-microtubule density in the anaphase spindle, representing the six sets of separating homologous chromosomes in C. elegans; this organization was clear in both early- (Figure 1D, Video 1) and mid-anaphase (Figure 2A, Videos 2–5).
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution imaging data shown in Figures 1D and 2A, and Videos 1-5.

claim: In late anaphase, chromosomes are found at the extreme ends of the microtubules at the spindle poles and the microtubule bundles in the center of the spindle converge, closing the channels.
source: In late anaphase, chromosomes are found at the extreme ends of the microtubules at the spindle poles and the microtubule bundles in the center of the spindle converge, closing the channels (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1C and 1E.

claim: Even in late anaphase, lateral microtubule bundles maintain contact with the chromosomes, splitting around them at the poles.
source: However, even at this stage, lateral microtubule bundles maintain contact with the chromosomes, splitting around them at the poles (Figure 1C,E, insets).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1C and 1E.

claim: The MPM-2 antibody marks the ring structures in both metaphase and anaphase in C. elegans oocytes.
source: First, we found that the MPM-2 antibody (raised against mitotic phospho-proteins [Davis et al., 1983]), which had been previously shown to stain the mid-region of meiotic bivalents (Kitagawa and Rose, 1999), marked the ring structures in both metaphase and anaphase (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 2A-C and citations to Davis et al., 1983 and Kitagawa and Rose, 1999.

claim: During anaphase, the MPM-2-marked rings completely dissociate from chromosomes and remain in the center of the spindle.
source: During anaphase, the MPM-2-marked rings completely dissociated from chromosomes and remained in the center of the spindle (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In mid-anaphase, the ring structures appear elongated but retain a ring-like appearance, suggesting that the rings flatten as anaphase progresses.
source: In mid-anaphase, these structures appeared elongated but retained a ring-like appearance (Figure 2B, asterisk), suggesting that the rings flatten as anaphase progresses, forming the bar-shaped structures previously described (Dumont et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Dumont et al., 2010.

claim: The ring structures are located within the six microtubule channels, with each open channel containing a pair of separating chromosomes with a disassembling ring between them.
source: Importantly, these structures were located within the six microtubule channels; each open channel contained a pair of separating chromosomes with a disassembling ring between them (Figure 2A, Videos 2–5).
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Videos 2-5.

claim: In late anaphase, MPM-2 staining is diffuse and other ring components are not discernable as distinct structures, suggesting that the rings have disassembled.
source: In late anaphase, at the stage where microtubule bundles in the central spindle converge (Figure 1C), MPM-2 staining was diffuse and other ring components were also not discernable as distinct structures, suggesting that the rings had disassembled (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SEP-1/separase localizes to cup-like structures surrounding bivalents and to filamentous structures found within the spindle in metaphase.
source: We found that when the rings were associated with chromosomes in metaphase, SEP-1 localized to cup-like structures surrounding bivalents and to filamentous structures found within the spindle (Figure 2C), a pattern also exhibited by meiotic kinetochore components (Monen et al., 2005), consistent with an earlier study (Bembenek et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C and citations to Monen et al., 2005 and Bembenek et al., 2007.

claim: During anaphase, SEP-1/separase localizes to the ring structures.
source: However, during anaphase, SEP-1 localized to the ring structures; this dramatic relocalization correlated with anaphase onset, as SEP-1 was found on the rings in early anaphase, when the spindle had rotated but chromosomes had barely separated (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Separase likely redistributes to the mid-region of meiotic chromosomes at anaphase onset to cleave cohesin and then remains associated with the ring structures during anaphase.
source: Therefore, separase likely redistributes to the mid-region of meiotic chromosomes at anaphase onset to cleave cohesin and then remains associated with the ring structures during anaphase, suggesting that ring removal from chromosomes is coordinated with cohesion release.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data of SEP-1 shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ring removal from chromosomes is coordinated with cohesion release.
source: Therefore, separase likely redistributes to the mid-region of meiotic chromosomes at anaphase onset to cleave cohesin and then remains associated with the ring structures during anaphase, suggesting that ring removal from chromosomes is coordinated with cohesion release.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data of SEP-1 shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In monopolar Meiosis I, the six bivalents move away from the central pole, oscillate, and then coordinately move inwards to the pole.
source: Live imaging of monopolar spindle dynamics demonstrated that in Meiosis I the six bivalents move away from the central pole, oscillate, and then coordinately move inwards to the pole (Figure 3A, Video 6); in most cases, polar body extrusion failed so all chromosomes were retained in the cell.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Video 6.

claim: In monopolar Meiosis II, the 12 separated chromosomes move away from the central pole, oscillate, and then move back in.
source: This behavior was then repeated in Meiosis II, with the 12 separated chromosomes moving out as the monopolar spindle forms, oscillating, and then moving back in (Figure 3B, Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Video 7.

claim: Separase colocalizes with ring components when chromosomes are located near the central pole in monopolar spindles, demonstrating that this configuration represents anaphase and not congression.
source: However, we found that separase colocalizes with ring components when the chromosomes are located near the central pole (Figure 3C), demonstrating that this configuration represents anaphase and not congression.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Following MCAK/KLP-7 depletion, monopolar spindles remain large in anaphase, but chromosomes still move inward.
source: Following MCAK depletion, monopolar spindles remained large in anaphase, but chromosomes still moved in (Figure 3D, top row), indicating that spindle shrinkage and microtubule depolymerization is not responsible for the inward movement.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Spindle shrinkage and microtubule depolymerization is not responsible for inward chromosome movement in monopolar anaphase.
source: Following MCAK depletion, monopolar spindles remained large in anaphase, but chromosomes still moved in (Figure 3D, top row), indicating that spindle shrinkage and microtubule depolymerization is not responsible for the inward movement.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that chromosomes move inward even when spindles remain large after MCAK depletion (Figure 3D).

claim: While chromosomes move inwards in monopolar anaphase, the ring structures are located out towards the periphery of the monopolar spindle, where the plus ends are located.
source: Importantly, we found that while chromosomes move inwards in monopolar anaphase, the ring structures could be observed out towards the periphery of the monopolar spindle, where the plus ends are located.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: In monopolar anaphase, rings are removed from chromosomes and remain near the plus ends, similar to bipolar anaphase where rings are left behind in the center of the spindle.
source: Therefore, similar to bipolar anaphase, where the rings are left behind in the center of the spindle, in monopolar anaphase they are also removed from chromosomes and remain near the plus ends, presumably where the chromosomes were located when anaphase was induced.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Under metaphase arrest on monopolar spindles, a plus-end directed force acts on the rings, causing them to stretch, and a counterbalancing minus-end force is exerted on the chromosome.
source: These observations are consistent with the interpretation that under metaphase arrest, a plus-end directed force acts on the rings, causing them to stretch, and a counterbalancing minus-end force is exerted on the chromosome, resisting the stretching force; when the ring predominantly stretches off of one side of the bivalent, this tug-of-war can cause the bivalents to rotate.
evidence: This is inferred from imaging data showing stretched rings on metaphase-arrested monopolar spindles (Figure 4A).

claim: Minus-end forces act on chromosomes prior to anaphase induction in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that minus end forces act on chromosomes prior to anaphase induction.
evidence: This is supported by observations of stretched rings and chromosome positioning in metaphase-arrested monopolar spindles (Figure 4).

claim: Minus-end forces accumulate under metaphase arrest, causing the rings to stretch and then ultimately be removed from the chromosomes as these increasing forces drive chromosomal movement to minus ends.
source: The fact that we observe a mixed population of structures suggests that these forces accumulate under metaphase arrest, causing the rings to stretch and then ultimately be removed from the chromosomes as these increasing forces drive chromosomal movement to minus ends.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of a mixed population of structures with varying degrees of ring stretching and chromosome positioning in metaphase-arrested monopolar spindles (Figure 4).

claim: Dynein localizes diffusely to the oocyte spindle during prometaphase and metaphase and then further concentrates at poles as the spindle rotates in preparation for anaphase.
source: Previously, dynein has been shown to localize diffusely to the oocyte spindle during prometaphase and metaphase and then further concentrate at poles as the spindle rotates in preparation for anaphase (Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ellefson and McNally, 2009 and van der Voet et al., 2009.

claim: A population of dynein cups meiotic chromosomes in C. elegans oocytes.
source: We confirmed this localization pattern, but we also detected a population of dynein that cupped meiotic chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Chromosomal dynein localization is more clearly visible on monopolar spindles than on bipolar spindles.
source: However, chromosomal localization was more clearly visible on monopolar spindles. Since chromosomes are spread out in these structures, the spindle pool of dynein was more separated from the chromosomal pool, allowing visualization of dynein cupping the bivalent ends (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Dynein is often seen asymmetrically localized on chromosomes, with stronger staining on the end of the bivalent pointing outwards towards the microtubule plus ends.
source: On these chromosomes, dynein was often seen asymmetrically localized, with stronger staining on the end of the bivalent pointing outwards towards the microtubule plus ends (asterisks), raising the possibility that dynein may preferentially load from this direction.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In anaphase, dynein is observed at the poleward surfaces of separating chromosomes, cupping the chromosomal surface, but is undetectable on the inside surfaces.
source: In anaphase, we observed dynein at the poleward surfaces of separating chromosomes, again cupping the chromosomal surface (Figure 5B), but undetectable on the inside surfaces (in the region where chromosomes would have been previously associated before release of cohesion).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Dynein moves from spindle poles towards the outside surfaces of chromosomes in anaphase.
source: These findings are in line with previous work that reported that dynein moves from spindle poles towards the outside surfaces of chromosomes in anaphase (Dumont et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2010.

claim: Dynein localizes to meiotic chromosomes both prior to and during anaphase, placing it in a location where it could provide a minus-end directed force during congression and segregation.
source: Therefore, dynein localizes to meiotic chromosomes both prior to and during anaphase, placing it in a location where it could provide a minus-end directed force during congression and segregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Following partial dynein depletion, significantly more chromosomes (60%) are found near the plus ends of microtubules on monopolar spindles compared to control (34%).
source: During normal monopolar spindle formation, chromosomes move out away from the pole and oscillate (Figure 3A,B, Videos 6, 7); in fixed images, we found that 34% of chromosomes were found near the plus ends of microtubules, reflecting this dynamic positioning (Figure 5C, gray bars). However, significantly more chromosomes (60%) were found in this location following dynein depletion (Figure 5C, black bars), suggesting that dynein generates a minus-end directed force on chromosomes that affects their positioning.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of chromosome positioning data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Dynein generates a minus-end directed force on chromosomes that affects their positioning.
source: However, significantly more chromosomes (60%) were found in this location following dynein depletion (Figure 5C, black bars), suggesting that dynein generates a minus-end directed force on chromosomes that affects their positioning.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that more chromosomes are positioned near plus ends following dynein depletion (Figure 5C).

claim: A significant fraction of monopolar anaphase spindles (15/21) have lagging chromosomes following treatment with low concentrations of ciliobrevin.
source: Consistent with this finding, we also observed lagging chromosomes on anaphase monopolar spindles following partial dynein inhibition. While chromosomes usually move coordinately to the pole in monopolar anaphase (Figure 3A,B), a significant fraction of spindles had some chromosomes towards microtubule plus ends upon treatment with low concentrations of ciliobrevin (Figure 5D; 15/21 monopolar anaphases), suggesting that dynein provides a minus-end directed force during anaphase as well as during congression.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Dynein provides a minus-end directed force during anaphase as well as during congression.
source: While chromosomes usually move coordinately to the pole in monopolar anaphase (Figure 3A,B), a significant fraction of spindles had some chromosomes towards microtubule plus ends upon treatment with low concentrations of ciliobrevin (Figure 5D; 15/21 monopolar anaphases), suggesting that dynein provides a minus-end directed force during anaphase as well as during congression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of lagging chromosomes following dynein inhibition (Figure 5D).

claim: Following brief dynein inactivation using the temperature-sensitive mutant dhc-1(ct76), a significant fraction of anaphase spindles have lagging chromosomes (2/12 after 5 min, 15/20 after 7.5 min, and 15/21 after 10 min shift).
source: Following brief dynein inactivation using this strategy, we observed a significant fraction of anaphase spindles that had lagging chromosomes (2/12 after a 5 min shift, 15/20 after a 7.5 min shift, and 15/21 after a 10 min shift), supporting a role for dynein in chromosome segregation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Dynein plays a role in chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Following brief dynein inactivation using this strategy, we observed a significant fraction of anaphase spindles that had lagging chromosomes (2/12 after a 5 min shift, 15/20 after a 7.5 min shift, and 15/21 after a 10 min shift), supporting a role for dynein in chromosome segregation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the observation of lagging chromosomes following dynein inactivation (Figure 5E).

claim: Univalent chromosomes in him-8(me4) and zim-2(tm574) mutants do not form ring structures.
source: These univalents were not recognized by antibodies against MPM-2 or the CPC component AIR-2/Aurora B, indicating that they do not form ring structures (Figure 6A, asterisks), and consequently each spindle had only five rings.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Univalent chromosomes are able to load kinetochore components.
source: However, the univalents were able to load kinetochore components, as BUB-1, which localizes to both the kinetochore and the ring (Monen et al., 2005; Dumont et al., 2010), coated their outer surfaces (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Monen et al., 2005 and Dumont et al., 2010.

claim: Univalents lack a plus-end directed force, as both univalents are located near the pole in every monopolar spindle quantified (40/40 spindles; 80/80 univalents).
source: Importantly, we found that univalents lacked a plus-end directed force, since in monopolar spindles both univalents were located near the pole in every spindle we quantified (40/40 spindles; 80/80 univalents) (Figure 6B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of univalent positioning on monopolar spindles shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Univalents exhibit congression defects on bipolar spindles, being fairly evenly distributed between zones 1, 2, and 3.
source: Moreover, we found that univalents exhibited congression defects on bipolar spindles. This phenotype was especially apparent following metaphase arrest, as most bivalents are aligned in those conditions, allowing us to more clearly quantify univalent position with relation to the metaphase plate (Figure 6B). For quantification, we assessed whether the univalent was found in the middle region of the spindle where the bivalents were located (Zone 1), close to but not completely overlapping with the bivalents (Zone 2), or in the regions closer to the poles (Zone 3). Univalents were fairly evenly distributed between these three categories, consistent with the univalents being positioned at random on bipolar spindles.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of univalent positioning on bipolar spindles shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Univalents remain as intact units during anaphase and do not release cohesion between sister chromatids.
source: Next, we assessed the behavior of univalents during anaphase. First, we found that univalents remained as intact units during anaphase and did not release cohesion between sister chromatids.
evidence: This is supported by observations of univalent behavior during anaphase (Figure 6C).

claim: Separase is not targeted to univalents, preventing cohesion release, because univalents lack ring components.
source: This observation is consistent with our finding that separase relocalizes to the rings at the metaphase to anaphase transition (Figure 2C); since univalents lack ring components (Figure 6A), separase is likely not targeted to them, preventing cohesion release.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that separase relocalizes to rings (Figure 2C) and univalents lack rings (Figure 6A).

claim: Most univalents (76%) lag during anaphase.
source: Most often, we found that these intact univalents lagged during anaphase (Figure 6C, top row; 76%).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of univalent behavior during anaphase shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 24% of univalents do not lag and instead appear to segregate with the rest of the chromosomes.
source: However, 24% of univalents did not lag and instead appeared to segregate with the rest of the chromosomes (Figure 6C, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of univalent behavior during anaphase shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The position of the univalent when anaphase is triggered determines its behavior during segregation.
source: These findings are consistent with the interpretation that the position of the univalent when anaphase is triggered determines its behavior during segregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some univalents segregate normally while others lag (Figure 6C).

claim: Univalents located close to a pole prior to segregation (zone 3) likely remain close to that same pole during anaphase and appear to segregate with the rest of the chromosomes.
source: Univalents that were located close to a pole prior to segregation (zone 3) likely remain close to that same pole during anaphase; minus-end forces could properly act on that univalent and therefore it would appear to segregate with the rest of the chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some univalents segregate normally (Figure 6C) and the positioning data (Figure 6B).

claim: A univalent located close to the chromosomes (zones 1 and 2) becomes trapped in the center, caught between overlapping bundles of microtubules, with minus-end forces acting on both sides pulling it in opposite directions.
source: However, a univalent located close to the chromosomes (zones 1 and 2) would become trapped in the center, as it would be caught between overlapping bundles of microtubules, with minus-end forces acting on both sides of the univalent pulling it in opposite directions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most univalents lag (Figure 6C) and the positioning data (Figure 6B).

claim: The behavior of univalents during congression and segregation supports a model in which a balance between opposing plus- and minus-end directed forces dictate chromosome position on the acentrosomal spindle.
source: Therefore, the behavior of univalents during congression and segregation supports a model in which a balance between opposing plus- and minus-end directed forces dictate chromosome position on the acentrosomal spindle and would represent a case in which the plus-end force is eliminated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations of univalent behavior (Figure 6).

claim: Chromosome segregation on the C. elegans acentrosomal spindle is driven by minus-end directed movement along lateral microtubule bundles.
source: Taken together, our data support a model in which chromosome segregation on the C. elegans acentrosomal spindle is driven by minus-end directed movement along lateral microtubule bundles (Figure 7A), revealing a new kinetochore-independent strategy for partitioning chromosomes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the data presented.

claim: The spindle reorganizes at the metaphase to anaphase transition by broadening the spindle poles and thereby creating channels that are open from pole to pole.
source: The spindle reorganizes at the metaphase to anaphase transition to enable this mode of segregation, by broadening the spindle poles and thereby creating channels that are open from pole to pole.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Chromosomes move through the open channels until they are located at the tips of the microtubules at the minus ends, at which point the channels close and the spindle disassembles.
source: Chromosomes move through these channels until they are located at the tips of the microtubules at the minus ends, at which point the channels close and the spindle disassembles.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Coupling spindle pole broadening to anaphase onset serves to open a path for chromosomes to move all the way to the microtubule minus ends.
source: Coupling spindle pole broadening to anaphase onset could potentially serve a dual purpose in regulating chromosome dynamics in the context of our model. First, pole broadening would be important in anaphase, as it would serve to open a path for chromosomes to move all the way to the microtubule minus ends.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed spindle reorganization.

claim: Having the poles more focused in prometaphase could bias chromosomal movement towards the metaphase plate.
source: Moreover, we speculate that having the poles more focused in prometaphase could serve the opposite purpose; since chromosomes move along lateral microtubule bundles during congression as well, having the poles 'closed' at that stage could bias chromosomal movement towards the metaphase plate.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the function of pole morphology.

claim: During congression, the ring provides a plus-end directed force that promotes movement to the metaphase plate and during the same period minus-end directed forces begin to accumulate on chromosomes.
source: We further propose that chromosome movement on acentrosomal spindles is mediated through a balance of plus- and minus-end directed forces operating on chromosomes (Figure 7B). During congression, the ring provides a plus-end directed force that promotes movement to the metaphase plate and during the same period minus-end directed forces begin to accumulate on chromosomes.
evidence: This is the proposed model supported by data from Figures 3-6.

claim: As chromosomes align at the metaphase plate, the plus- and minus-end directed forces are each balanced, since chromosomes are positioned within microtubule bundles of overlapping polarity.
source: As chromosomes then align at the metaphase plate, the plus- and minus-end directed forces would each be balanced, since at that stage the chromosomes are positioned within microtubule bundles of overlapping polarity, with both plus- and minus-ends on each side.
evidence: This is inferred from the model and the observed chromosome positioning.

claim: Minus-end forces are likely weak early in congression and then accumulate in preparation for anaphase.
source: Since our data support the idea that minus-end forces increase as metaphase progresses, we infer that these forces are likely weak early in congression (allowing plus-end forces to be dominant) and then accumulate in preparation for anaphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the metaphase arrest data (Figure 4) and dynein localization patterns (Figure 5).

claim: Once anaphase is triggered, ring removal alters the balance of forces, enabling minus-end forces to propel separated chromosomes to the poles.
source: Once anaphase is triggered, ring removal alters the balance of forces, enabling minus-end forces to propel separated chromosomes to the poles.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism supported by data from Figures 2-6.

claim: The proposed mechanism directly couples key essential events at the metaphase to anaphase transition, as cleavage of cohesin by separase facilitates ring removal from chromosomes, thereby also removing a plus-end directed force.
source: Importantly, our proposed mechanism would directly couple key essential events at the metaphase to anaphase transition, as cleavage of cohesin by separase would also facilitate ring removal from chromosomes, thereby also removing a plus-end directed force.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that separase relocalizes to rings at anaphase onset (Figure 2C).

claim: The outcome of the proposed mechanism is coordinated poleward movement, driving chromosome segregation.
source: Consequently, the outcome would be coordinated poleward movement, driving chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is the conclusion of the proposed model.

claim: A previous model proposed that spindle poles disassemble at anaphase onset and a new microtubule array polymerizes between separating chromosomes to push them apart.
source: A previous study proposed a different model for kinetochore-independent segregation, where the metaphase spindle disassembles from the poles and then a new microtubule array assembles between separating chromosomes, stimulated by ring component CLASP (CLS-2). In this model, a force provided by polymerizing microtubules pushing against the inside surface of separating chromosomes is the primary candidate driving segregation (Dumont et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2010.

claim: The current findings are not consistent with the previous model where a new microtubule array polymerizes between separating chromosomes to push them apart.
source: Our findings are not consistent with key features of this model, since spindle poles do not appear to disassemble and polymerization of a new microtubule array coupled to the inside surfaces of separating chromosomes would be predicted to close the microtubule channels that we observe.
evidence: This is based on the observation that poles remain intact (Figure 1B) and channels remain open (Figures 1D, 2A).

claim: The previous model does not account for the behavior of chromosomes during monopolar anaphase, where separated chromosomes move together to the same pole.
source: Moreover, the previous model also does not account for the behavior of chromosomes during monopolar anaphase, where separated chromosomes do not move apart, pushed from the center, but instead move together to the same pole, leaving the ring behind.
evidence: This is based on the monopolar anaphase data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Spindle elongation likely contributes to segregation in C. elegans oocytes, potentially driven by CLASP-dependent microtubule polymerization.
source: However, the major length changes that occur in the C. elegans oocyte spindle (with it shrinking and then elongating as anaphase progresses) make it likely that spindle elongation also contributes to segregation, potentially driven by CLASP-dependent microtubule polymerization as this previous study proposed.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on observed spindle dynamics and previous work.

claim: Spindle elongation in C. elegans oocytes may be analogous to Anaphase B in mitotically dividing cells.
source: This process may be analogous to Anaphase B in mitotically dividing cells (where spindle pole separation drives sets of separating chromosomes further apart [Walczak and Heald, 2008]) but it would have to occur within the context of the unique spindle organization that we have now defined, with lateral microtubule bundles extending alongside separating chromosome pairs.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning with citation to Walczak and Heald, 2008.

claim: Forces operating on the chromosomes themselves drive poleward movement in C. elegans oocytes.
source: However, even if spindle elongation contributes to segregation, our studies have now revealed another mechanism that operates in parallel, with forces operating on the chromosomes themselves driving poleward movement.
evidence: This is supported by all the data presented in the study.

claim: The segregation mechanism described could be viewed as analogous to Anaphase A, but is mechanistically distinct from what occurs in mitotically dividing cells.
source: This segregation mechanism could be viewed as analogous to Anaphase A, but it would be mechanistically distinct from what occurs in mitotically dividing cells, as the chromosome to pole movement that we have described does not require kinetochores and is instead mediated by motor-driven movement along lateral microtubule bundles.
evidence: This is based on the findings of the study and comparison to known mechanisms.

claim: An additional mechanism may exist to give the separating chromosomes an initial push apart to escape the zone of overlapping microtubules.
source: Although dynein is asymmetrically localized on separating chromosomes (as we do not detect it on the inside surface), it is still possible that some motors could associate with microtubule bundles oriented towards the incorrect pole (Figure 7B). Therefore, we speculate that an additional mechanism may exist to give the separating chromosomes an initial push apart; this mechanism could involve a morphological change in the ring structure as it is removed (a constriction or elongation), a small amount of CLASP-dependent microtubule polymerization, or a currently undiscovered mechanism.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: The rings could serve as physical barriers between separating chromosomes, blocking the center of the channel and preventing chromosomes from moving in the wrong direction.
source: It is also possible that the rings could simply serve as physical barriers between separating chromosomes, blocking the center of the channel and therefore preventing chromosomes from moving in the wrong direction, giving motors associated with properly oriented microtubule bundles an advantage.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Asymmetric dynein localization on monopolar spindles could reflect a loading mechanism where dynein walks towards the chromosomal surface from the microtubule plus ends.
source: We speculate that this asymmetric pattern could reflect the mechanism by which dynein loads onto the chromosomes, for example, if it walks towards the chromosomal surface from the microtubule plus ends.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed localization pattern (Figure 5A).

claim: Dynein loading from plus ends could facilitate accumulation of the motor on the outer surfaces of chromosomes prior to anaphase.
source: This loading mechanism could possibly facilitate accumulation of the motor on the outer surfaces of chromosomes prior to anaphase, since when chromosomes are at the metaphase plate with overlapping plus ends nearby, dynein loading via this mechanism might be especially efficient, allowing the motor to accumulate on chromosomes in preparation for anaphase initiation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the function of the proposed loading mechanism.

claim: Residual dynein activity following partial inhibition could explain why some chromosomes still exhibit poleward movement.
source: However, these phenotypes were not completely penetrant, as some chromosomes did exhibit poleward movement in each of these cases. One possibility is that this movement is due to residual dynein activity; since dynein also plays a role in spindle assembly, we had to use partial inactivation or a fast-acting temperature-sensitive mutant and each of these strategies could potentially leave a significant pool of active dynein.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the incomplete penetrance of dynein inhibition phenotypes.

claim: There may be additional factors contributing to the minus-end force operating on chromosomes, such as poleward flux or other minus-end directed motors.
source: A second possibility is that there are additional factors contributing to the minus-end force operating on chromosomes (for example, poleward flux or other minus-end directed motors).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential additional mechanisms.

claim: There may be multiple components of the plus-end directed force acting on chromosomes in addition to KLP-19.
source: This second possibility could also apply to the plus-end directed force; we previously demonstrated that the kinesin motor KLP-19 in the ring provides a polar ejection force using our monopolar spindle assay (Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009), but it is possible that other factors operate in parallel to promote congression.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning with citation to previous work (Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009).

claim: Even if there are multiple components of either the plus- or minus-end directed forces, the proposed mechanism for segregation with a hand-off between these forces could still operate as proposed.
source: However, even if there are multiple components of either the plus- or minus-end directed forces acting on chromosomes, the mechanism that we propose for segregation, with a hand-off between these forces, could still operate as proposed (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is reasoning about the robustness of the proposed model.

claim: Partial dynein inhibition results in especially large monopolar spindles (approximately 50% larger than normal).
source: Another interesting observation that emerged from our studies is that partial dynein inhibition results in especially large monopolar spindles (Figure 5C, the spindles shown are approximately 50% larger than normal monopolar spindles), suggesting that dynein also regulates spindle length.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Dynein regulates spindle length in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Another interesting observation that emerged from our studies is that partial dynein inhibition results in especially large monopolar spindles (Figure 5C, the spindles shown are approximately 50% larger than normal monopolar spindles), suggesting that dynein also regulates spindle length.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of larger spindles following dynein inhibition (Figure 5C).

claim: Dynein depletion has been reported to cause larger spindles in other systems.
source: A full understanding of this phenotype will require further experimentation, though our observation is consistent with work in other systems, where dynein depletion has also been reported to cause larger spindles (Gaetz and Kapoor, 2004; Morales-Mulia and Scholey, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gaetz and Kapoor, 2004 and Morales-Mulia and Scholey, 2005.

claim: Lateral interactions between kinetochores and microtubules occur before forming end-on attachments in mitotically dividing cells.
source: Notably, lateral interactions have been previously described in mitotically dividing cells and have been shown to play a role in chromosome congression. For example, kinetochores associate laterally with microtubules before forming end-on attachments (Tanaka, 2012), a class of kinesins on chromosome arms promotes congression (Vanneste et al., 2011), and chromosomes can congress under experimental conditions where kinetochore-fiber formation is inhibited (Cai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tanaka, 2012.

claim: A class of kinesins on chromosome arms promotes congression in mitotically dividing cells.
source: Notably, lateral interactions have been previously described in mitotically dividing cells and have been shown to play a role in chromosome congression. For example, kinetochores associate laterally with microtubules before forming end-on attachments (Tanaka, 2012), a class of kinesins on chromosome arms promotes congression (Vanneste et al., 2011), and chromosomes can congress under experimental conditions where kinetochore-fiber formation is inhibited (Cai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vanneste et al., 2011.

claim: Chromosomes can congress under experimental conditions where kinetochore-fiber formation is inhibited.
source: Notably, lateral interactions have been previously described in mitotically dividing cells and have been shown to play a role in chromosome congression. For example, kinetochores associate laterally with microtubules before forming end-on attachments (Tanaka, 2012), a class of kinesins on chromosome arms promotes congression (Vanneste et al., 2011), and chromosomes can congress under experimental conditions where kinetochore-fiber formation is inhibited (Cai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cai et al., 2009.

claim: Lateral microtubule-chromosome associations can be the primary drivers of chromosome movement in an unperturbed system.
source: However, our work now demonstrates that these associations can be the primary drivers of chromosome movement in an unperturbed system, and that in addition to congression, they can also provide the force to power chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study supported by all the data presented.

claim: Lateral microtubule-chromosome associations can provide the force to power chromosome segregation.
source: However, our work now demonstrates that these associations can be the primary drivers of chromosome movement in an unperturbed system, and that in addition to congression, they can also provide the force to power chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study supported by all the data presented.

claim: Acentrosomal spindles in mouse oocytes don't have end-on kinetochore microtubule-attachments prior to achieving metaphase alignment.
source: Interestingly, our findings also have parallels with previous work on the mammalian oocyte spindle. First, it has been shown that acentrosomal spindles in mouse oocytes don't have end-on kinetochore microtubule-attachments prior to achieving metaphase alignment (Brunet et al., 1999), and fluorescence imaging of prometaphase is suggestive of the presence of lateral microtubule bundles surrounding the chromosomes (with a lower density of microtubules at the ends) (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brunet et al., 1999.

claim: Fluorescence imaging of prometaphase in mouse oocytes is suggestive of the presence of lateral microtubule bundles surrounding the chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, our findings also have parallels with previous work on the mammalian oocyte spindle. First, it has been shown that acentrosomal spindles in mouse oocytes don't have end-on kinetochore microtubule-attachments prior to achieving metaphase alignment (Brunet et al., 1999), and fluorescence imaging of prometaphase is suggestive of the presence of lateral microtubule bundles surrounding the chromosomes (with a lower density of microtubules at the ends) (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007.

claim: Kinetochore-microtubule attachments are established after metaphase alignment in mouse oocytes.
source: While kinetochore-microtubule attachments are established after metaphase alignment (Brunet et al., 1999; Kitajima et al., 2011) and have been demonstrated during anaphase (FitzHarris, 2012), there is also evidence for kinetochore-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brunet et al., 1999 and Kitajima et al., 2011.

claim: Kinetochore-microtubule attachments have been demonstrated during anaphase in mouse oocytes.
source: While kinetochore-microtubule attachments are established after metaphase alignment (Brunet et al., 1999; Kitajima et al., 2011) and have been demonstrated during anaphase (FitzHarris, 2012), there is also evidence for kinetochore-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to FitzHarris, 2012.

claim: DNA-coated beads injected into mouse oocytes form acentrosomal spindles and exhibit dynein-dependent poleward movements when anaphase is induced.
source: An intriguing study reported that DNA-coated beads injected into mouse oocytes formed acentrosomal spindles and that when anaphase was induced, these beads exhibited dynein-dependent poleward movements (Deng et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Deng et al., 2009.

claim: The mechanism described in this study could also operate in mammalian oocytes during anaphase.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the mechanism that we describe could also operate in mammalian oocytes during anaphase.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on parallels with previous work on mammalian oocytes.

claim: In mammalian oocytes, lateral microtubule associations established to promote congression could remain intact in anaphase, and dynein localized on the chromosomes could provide a force to help move chromosomes along these microtubules towards minus ends.
source: Although the primary driver of chromosome-to-pole movement in these cells may be the canonical kinetochore-driven mechanism, lateral microtubule associations established to promote congression could remain intact in anaphase, and dynein localized on the chromosomes could provide a force to help move chromosomes along these microtubules towards minus ends.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms in mammalian oocytes.

claim: The mechanism revealed in this study may be widely applicable to understanding chromosome behavior during oocyte meiosis.
source: Therefore, by studying anaphase in C. elegans oocytes, we have revealed a new mechanism driving chromosome segregation on acentrosomal spindles that may be widely applicable to understanding chromosome behavior during oocyte meiosis.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: At the metaphase to anaphase transition in C. elegans oocytes, the spindle rotates until it is perpendicular to the cortex.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that a number of events occur concomitantly at the metaphase to anaphase transition: (1) the spindle rotates until it is perpendicular to the cortex, (2) the spindle shrinks dramatically, and (3) the poles broaden.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and citations to previous studies (Albertson and Thomson, 1993; Yang et al., 2003; McNally and McNally, 2005; McNally et al., 2006).

claim: At the metaphase to anaphase transition in C. elegans oocytes, the spindle shrinks dramatically.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that a number of events occur concomitantly at the metaphase to anaphase transition: (1) the spindle rotates until it is perpendicular to the cortex, (2) the spindle shrinks dramatically, and (3) the poles broaden.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and citations to previous studies (Albertson and Thomson, 1993; Yang et al., 2003; McNally and McNally, 2005; McNally et al., 2006).

claim: At the metaphase to anaphase transition in C. elegans oocytes, the spindle poles broaden.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that a number of events occur concomitantly at the metaphase to anaphase transition: (1) the spindle rotates until it is perpendicular to the cortex, (2) the spindle shrinks dramatically, and (3) the poles broaden.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and citations to previous studies (Albertson and Thomson, 1993; Yang et al., 2003; McNally and McNally, 2005; McNally et al., 2006).

claim: As anaphase progresses in C. elegans oocytes, the spindle elongates again after initially shrinking.
source: Then, as anaphase progresses, the spindle elongates again (Albertson and Thomson, 1993; Yang et al., 2003; McNally and McNally, 2005; McNally et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albertson and Thomson, 1993; Yang et al., 2003; McNally and McNally, 2005; McNally et al., 2006.
